summary: Tata Research describes a Google Cloud framework that turns natural-language cloud-engineering requests into a generated repository plus a verified deployment. It separates 'graph engineering' (an author-defined workflow graph whose transitions require machine-checkable repository, deployment and runtime evidence), 'loop engineering' (bounded diagnose, repair or re-plan, retry, re-verify) and a zero-trust harness (IAM/WIF, OPA, gVisor sandboxes, MCP-scoped tools). On a self-built benchmark of 140 greenfield tasks across 14 domains under six injected conditions (3,360 executions over four models), verified completion ranges from 56.4% (Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite) to 95.0% (GPT-5.6 Sol). Gate, denial and termination metrics are 100% for every model because deterministic control code enforces them. Two same-model ablations are the only comparisons.

claims.claim: The framework turns NL cloud tasks into verified deployments (VTCR 56.4-95.0% across four models).
claims.evidence: Table 2: 79, 96, 115 and 133 of 140 nominal executions. The benchmark is author-built, with no external agent or plain-loop baseline (e.g. Gemini CLI or Codex on the same tasks), a single execution per task-condition, and no variance. All tasks are greenfield synthesis; modifying existing systems is future work (§6.4).

claims.claim: Removing the bounded recovery loop collapses completion (95.0% to 12.9%).
claims.evidence: Table 9, Ablation 1: GPT-5.6 Sol, the same 140 nominal tasks with graph, harness and verification held fixed, and Reflection/Diagnosis + Repair/Re-plan disabled. This is an isolating same-model comparison. Single run, one model.

claims.claim: Machine-checkable verification gates eliminate the residual invalid transitions seen under model-determined progression.
claims.evidence: Table 9, Ablation 2: 420/420 vs 416/420 perturbation executions blocked (4 invalid progressions: 1 deployment, 3 runtime). The difference is small. By reviewer computation, a two-sided Fisher exact test on 0/420 vs 4/420 gives p≈0.12. The effect of those 4 progressions on final outcomes is not reported.

claims.claim: Evidence gating, authorization and bounded termination hold across models and domains (EGER/UCDR/BTR 100%, ACPR 99.3%).
claims.evidence: Tables 3, 6-8. The authors note these are 'framework-enforced' and model-invariant. They measure whether deterministic gate and policy code fired on author-injected conditions, not whether the agent is safe under adversarial inputs (§6.3: 'limited adversarial testing'). The identical 139/140 ACPR for every model shows a fixed policy decision, not a measured property.

patterns.note: The most direct P36 test in this batch. An author-defined workflow graph (understand, plan, generate, test, diagnose/repair, re-test, security review, next stage) with evidence-gated transitions, run by an ADK Graph Orchestrator. Isolating comparison (Ablation 2): same model (GPT-5.6 Sol), budget, tasks and evidence, with progression decided by the model instead of the graph. Static gating wins directionally (0 vs 4/420 invalid transitions) but the gap is not significant (Fisher two-sided p≈0.12, reviewer-computed), and the effect on final completion is unreported. Read: the hard gate removes a residual ~1% of premature transitions that a strong model mostly avoids on its own when given the same evidence. No comparison against a plain agent loop without any graph.

Ablation 1, same model, tasks and harness: disabling the execution-verification-driven repair loop drops verified completion from 95.0% to 12.9%. The loop, not the graph, carries most of the completion rate. Single run, one model; the counterfactual is one-shot execution.

OPA Gatekeeper, RBAC/ABAC and per-action authorization deny 140/140 injected out-of-scope requests and permit 139/140 authorized ones identically for every model. This shows deterministic enforcement by construction, not robustness; there is no adversarial or bypass testing (§6.3).
Recovery is bounded at 20 attempts, 120 min, 10M tokens and 500 tool calls, and BTR is 100% under forced exhaustion. No token or dollar consumption is reported for any condition.
gVisor GKE Sandbox and VS Code/Chrome sandboxes are described, not evaluated separately.
Approval gates for consequential actions are mentioned; no human-in-the-loop measurement.
Specialised agents (repository generation, review, deployment, verification, monitoring) over A2A; no single-agent comparison.
OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Cloud Logging/Trace plus retained evidence for audit; not evaluated.
The workflow graph is author-defined. The model may return revised execution plans from the repair path, but the graph orchestrator chooses transitions; no LLM-emitted task DAG is evaluated.

methodology.sample: 140 author-constructed greenfield NL tasks (10 per domain x 14 domains) x 6 controlled conditions = 840 executions per model; 3,360 total.
methodology.baselines: None external. Two internal ablations on GPT-5.6 Sol only: no recovery loop, and model-determined progression.
methodology.models: Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.6 Sol, at provider defaults.
methodology.variance: Single execution per task-condition; no CIs or repeats.
methodology.ablations: Recovery loop off (VTCR 95.0 to 12.9); verification-gated vs model-determined progression (EGER 100 to 99.0).
methodology.contamination_controls: Isolated per-execution resources against cross-run leakage. Tasks are new, so benchmark contamination is not applicable, but they were written by the system's authors.
methodology.languages: Not specified per task: generated repositories, CI/CD, IaC (Terraform/Argo CD) on Google Cloud.

standards.artifacts: No code, benchmark or prompts released; task families are only summarised (Table 10).

biases.detail: The authors wrote the benchmark, the perturbations, the metrics and the system.
EGER, UCDR and BTR measure whether deterministic control code fired on injected conditions. 100% shows the gates are wired, not that agent behaviour is safe or correct.
No comparison with a plain agent loop or an existing agent product on the same tasks, so the framework's net value over a strong model with tests is unmeasured.
One run per task-condition; the ablation difference is 4/420 with no significance test.
Budgets are stated but token and dollar usage is not reported, even for the 95% vs 12.9% ablation.
Neither the benchmark nor the code is released.
The abstract claims a 'unified engineering architecture' for DevOps, CloudOps, SRE, SecOps, DataOps, MLOps, AgentOps and RAG on a greenfield, single-cloud, author-built benchmark.

coi.affiliations: Tata Research Development and Design Centre (TCS).
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Google Cloud services (ADK, GKE, gVisor) as substrate, and Gemini/GPT models; no TCS product is graded.
coi.funding: Not stated; experiments used Google Cloud Free Trial credits.
coi.detail: An IT-services vendor describing its own framework; no proprietary product is ranked against competitors.

verdict_reason: Admitted for two same-model ablations that isolate a static evidence-gated graph and a bounded repair loop. That is rare in this corpus and on point for the batch question. Caveats: no external baseline, one run per cell, an author-built greenfield benchmark, no released artifacts, and headline 100% figures that measure deterministic gate code rather than agent capability. The graph-gating ablation's margin (0 vs 4/420) is not statistically significant.
applicability: For the Java multi-repo team the paper gives a narrow but usable answer. With a strong model, a static state machine with evidence-gated transitions (build passes, deploy verified, runtime check green) adds a hard guarantee against the last ~1% of premature 'done' transitions, about 4 in 420 here. That matters most where an ingested healthcare-education artefact must not ship unverified. Most of the completion rate (95% vs 13%) comes from the bounded diagnose-repair-retest loop, which a plain agent with a test runner already has. A practical design is a small developer-defined gate graph across repositories (spec agreed, then per-repo build/tests, contract checks, integration verification) with bounded retry budgets, letting the agent act freely inside each node. It does not show that a heavier graph orchestrator beats a plain host loop with the same tests, and it covers greenfield generation on one cloud, not changes to existing Java repositories.

conflicts_with.detail: LLM-as-Code argues the model should never decide control flow because sampled sequencing is structurally unreliable. Here, model-determined progression with the same evidence was 99.0% correct vs 100% for the hard gate, a much smaller reliability gap than that thesis implies.

That source survey finds production coding harnesses are hand-rolled iterative loops with no workflow-graph framework. This paper argues an explicit workflow graph is the core of reliable long-horizon execution, though its own ablation attributes most completion to the loop.
